Testimony of Rep. Deqa Dhalac in support of
LD 1861, An Act to Require Training on Textured Hair for Aestheticians,
Barber Hair Stylists, Cosmetologists and Hair Designers
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor

Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Labor, I am Deqa Dhalac, and I am honored to represent House District 120, which includes
part of South Portland. I am here today to express my strong support for LD 1861, An Act to
Require Training on Textured Hair for Aestheticians, Barber Hair Stylists, Cosmetologists
and Hair Designers.

This bill would ensure that students entering the hairstyling profession receive training in the care and styling of textured and curly hair.
From personal experience, I know how difficult it can be to find professionals in Maine who are
knowledgeable about working with textured hair. This lack of expertise can be both frustrating and isolating for individuals with textured or curly hair.

But beyond feelings of exclusion, the lack of proper training can lead to real harm. Improper handling such as over-processing or overly tight braiding can result in significant hair damage or
even hair loss.

Often, all it takes is a little exposure to the specific needs of textured hair to make a big
difference. I've had to guide stylists myself during appointments. While I am comfortable
advocating for my needs, many people are not. A small amount of training can go a long way
toward making all clients feel safe, understood and respected.

LD 1861 simply directs the department to ensure that training for hair professionals includes
instruction on working with textured and curly hair. It does not increase the number of required hours, alter testing procedures or affect current licensing. The bill gives the department the flexibility to implement this within existing structures and resources.

With this bill, Maine has an opportunity to join a growing number of states including Louisiana,
New York, Connecticut, Minnesota, California and Washington that have taken similar steps to ensure inclusive, safe training standards. New Jersey and Vermont are also considering similar
legislation.

Thank you for your time and thoughtful consideration of this important issue. I respectfully urge
you to support LD 1861. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

Dear Chairman Tipping and Honorable Members of the Senate Committee on Labor,
On behalf of the Professional Beauty Association (PBA) we express our support for LD 1861/SP0731. LD 1861 will require a person applying for an individual license to practice as a cosmetologist, hair technician, manager, or instructor to complete training and have experience providing services on all hair textures, including coil, curl, or wave patterns, hair strand thicknesses, and volumes of hair. The legislation will ensure safe and sanitary texture hair care services are provided by educated, trained, and licensed beauty professionals in Maine.
According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics overall employment of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists is projected to grow 8 percent from 2022 to 2032, faster than the average for all occupations. About 89,400 openings for barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are projected each year, on average, over the decade. As the industry continues to grow and change, skills are refocused to meet the demands of consumers while maintaining health and safety.
The Texture Education Collective, an initiative of the Professional Beauty Association, is an alliance of professional hair industry leaders working to ensure cosmetology state licensing requirements and curriculum are inclusive of all hair textures and all hair types. Licensed professionals are trained and required to provide safe services. Consumers have a reasonable expectation to receive safe services in a sanitary environment. The proposed legislation fully aligns with our mission, and we commend the sponsors and the state of Maine for taking this essential step towards safety and inclusivity. This legislation is critical considering:
� Seventy-five percent of stylists express a desire for more training in styling textured hair. � Sixty-five percent of the world's consumer population has textured hair, a market of one billion people.
With the passage of this legislation, Maine will be at the forefront of promoting a more inclusive profession and experience for consumers. The Texture Education Collective urges the honorable members of the Committee and the Maine legislature to support and pass this legislation. It represents a significant stride towards creating an industry that can safely meet the needs of every individual, fostering inclusion, understanding, and ensuring safe services.

Good afternoon, Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and Members of the Committee. My name is
Penny Vaillancourt, and I am the Deputy Commissioner of DPFR. Thank you for the opportunity to
provide testimony on behalf of the Office of Professional and Occupational Regulation ("OPOR"). The
longtime OPOR manager who managed Barbering and Cosmetology Program ("BC") retired last week and we are currently without a manager of this program and five other programs under her unit. We are
actively recruiting.
This bill amends the Barbering and Cosmetology Licensure Act to require OPOR to adopt by rule a
requirement for cosmetology schools to include content specific to the care, styling and treatment of coiled,
curly or wavy hair, which is defined in the bill as "textured hair." Cosmetology schools train aestheticians,
barber hair stylists, cosmetologists and hair designers.
It is our understanding that the intent of the bill is not to increase the number of cosmetology hours
required for licensure but rather to require that the existing hours include training in textured hair. We will
leave it to the schools to respond to whether textured hair is currently part of their curriculum and what impact if any the proposed change would have on their curriculum or length of study.
OPOR/BC Rules 02 O41 Chapter 27 governs licensing of BC schools, which I have attached. As you can
see in the description of required curriculum on pages 70-75, the curriculum is described very generally.
We note that the rule sets for recommended -- not required curriculum. Specific requirements like those proposed in LD 1861 could potentially be achieved by defining textured hair and then adding textured hair
to each of the categories describing the curriculum and additionally stating that it was a required component of training.

'
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor
May 6, 2025
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Labor, I am Senator Rachel Talbot Ross. I represent Senate District 28, which includes part of my hometown of Portland and Peaks Island. Thank you for the opportunity to present LD 1861, "An Act to
Require Training on Textured Hair for Aestheticians, Barber Hair Stylists, Cosmetologists and Hair
Designers."

The bill is simple but critical: it directs the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation to include training in textured and curly hair in the training required to work as a hairstylist in Maine. Importantly, this bill would not impact existing licenses and would not require additional hours or even changes to the examination. It simply directs the Commissioner to ensure that curly and textured hair training is included in courses, and the bill leaves it up to the Commissioner to determine the best ways
to do that. I am open to any amendments to the bill that the department may suggest to clean up
terminology or ensure that the intent of this bill can be implemented.
For so many Mainers, this bill is also essential. Until now, many individuals have struggled to find hairstylists who know how to work with curly and textured hair. When mistakes are made that impact the aesthetics of a haircut, it can affect the morale of the person receiving that cut. When this experience becomes an institutional pattern from stylist to stylist, the same customer may feel marginalized and less
valued than other customers. This is demoralizing and can impact one's self-esteem and feelings of
belonging.
As a young child growing up in Maine, I can personally attest to this impact as it substantially affected how I, along with generations of women of color, understand beauty, leading to internalized standards
that felt unattainable -- like our natural hair was somehow less beautiful or acceptable.
Beyond that, however, is the very real health danger posed by stylists who are inexperienced and untrained in working with curly or textured hair. Indeed, we know that inexperience with braiding
textured hair can lead to traction alopecia (the hair falling out of the head). This often happens from excess tension or from leaving braids in too long. inexperience with coloring or lightening services for textured hair can alter the curl pattern and weaken the hair. Highly textured hair is more susceptible to
